NumPy is the fundamental package for scientific computing in Python. It is a Python library that provides a multidimensional array & matrices, mathematical, logical, shape manipulation, sorting, selecting, I/O, discrete Fourier transforms, basic linear algebra, basic statistical operations and much more.

Pandas is a fast, powerful, flexible and easy to use open source data analysis and manipulation tool, built on top of the Python programming language.

Matplotlib is a comprehensive library for creating static, animated, and interactive visualizations in Python.

Seaborn is a Python data visualization library based on matplotlib. It provides a high-level interface for drawing attractive and informative statistical graphics.

Warnings module is useful to alert the user of some condition in a program, where filterwarnings('ignore') filters all the warnings & ignores them.

In [1]:
# importing all the above mentioned libraries
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import warnings as wr
wr.filterwarnings('ignore')

adfuller (augmented dicky fuller) test is used to check stationarity of the data. A time series is said to be stationary when its statistical properties do not change w.r.t. time.

H0: unit root is present in the data => Non stationary

H1: unit root is not present in the data => stationary

The null and alternate hypothesis for the KPSS test are opposite that of the ADF test

kpss test is also used to check the stationarity of the data. H0: The data is stationary. H1: The data is non stationary

In null hypothesis testing, the criterion is called α (alpha) and is almost always set to 0.05. If there is less than a 5% chance of a result as extreme as the sample result if the null hypothesis were true, then the null hypothesis is rejected. When this happens, the result is said to be statistically significant.

A p value is used in hypothesis testing to help you support or reject the null hypothesis. The p value is the evidence against a null hypothesis. The smaller the p-value, the stronger the evidence that you should reject the null hypothesis.

A small p (≤ 0.05), reject the null hypothesis. This is strong evidence that the null hypothesis is invalid.

A large p (> 0.05) means the alternate hypothesis is weak, so you do not reject the null.

An Auto Correlation Function (ACF) determines the average correlation between a time series observation & its past value for different lag. But it failes to calculate actual correlation between two particular observations(t3 & t1) as it takes all the values that exist within them(t1,t2,t3). To solve this issue Partial auto correlation function (PACF) has been introduced which only gives correlation between two particular observations(t1 & t3).

In [2]:
# importing adfuller & kpss libraries from statsmodels package 
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools            import  adfuller
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools            import kpss


# importing the pacf library from statsmodels package to check correlation b/w observations with its previous observations
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools            import  pacf

# importing the acf library from statsmodels package to check correlation b/w the errors with its previous errors
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools            import  acf

# importing plot_pacf library from statsmodels package to plot pacf result
from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots        import  plot_pacf

# importing plot_acf library from statsmodels package to plot acf result
from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots        import  plot_acf

# import seasonal_decompose library from statsmodels package to check trend, seasonality & residual natures of the data
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal             import  seasonal_decompose

# import mean squared error & mean absolute percentage error from sklearn package
from sklearn.metrics                      import mean_squared_error, mean_absolute_percentage_error

# import ARIMA library from statsmodels package to use it to make AR, MA, ARMA & ARIMA models
from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model          import  ARIMA

We would like to filter only the records with components failure. Hence we drop the records that contains no failure. Then we would create consecutive datetime & group the failure records as per datetime. Other telemetry readings like volt, rotation, pressure, vibration will also be taken into consideration. We will count the component failure & calculate means for other telemetry readings.

In [15]:
# creating a dataframe with the grouped data
comp_failure_ts.index= pd.to_datetime(comp_failure_ts.index)

Creating an array with consecutive datetime with hour lag of an hour for an entire year. Then the values of the main components failure dataframe will be imposed on this array so that the component failure data gets updated w.r.t. the array. Then the records with mising values will be filled by backfilling(for most of the data) & front filling (for the last few records as there would be no record left to back fill) to avoid the presence of missing values.

In [16]:
# setting the start date as the very first datetime index
start = comp_failure_ts.index[0].date()

# setting the end date as one less than the total length of the datetime records
end = comp_failure_ts.index[len(comp_failure_ts)-1].date()

# creating the array with datetime for an entire year with a gap of each hour
new_dates = pd.date_range(start=start,end=end,freq='H')

We will consider the all the data occurring before 2015-10-31 as the training set & all data after the date is the testing set & create training & testing dataframes.

In [27]:
# splitting the data as training & testing sets
df_train = df_ts[df_ts.index < pd.to_datetime('2015-10-31')]
df_test = df_ts[df_ts.index >= pd.to_datetime('2015-10-31')]
In [28]:
# checking the count of rows & columns for both training & testing datasets
print(f'Train shape: {df_train.shape} & Test shape: {df_test.shape}')

Train shape: (7248, 5) & Test shape: (1465, 5)

Time Series = Trend + Seasonal + Residual

Trend implies Upward or Downward pattern of the data

Seasonality implies Repeating patterns of the data

Residual or error implies (Time Series - Trend - Seasonality)

In [29]:
# seasonal_decomposition library will calculate the trend, seasonality & residual values of the components failed
decomp_fail = seasonal_decompose(df_ts['failure'])

plt.show()
In [34]:
### using the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test for stationarity check

adf_test = adfuller(df_ts['failure'])

print('ADF Statistic: %f' % adf_test[0])
print('Critical Values @ 0.05: %.2f' % adf_test[4]['5%'])
print('p-value: %f' % adf_test[1])
print(adf_test)

Since p<0.05. Hence we reject the H0 for ADF test which implies the data is stationary.

Calculate RMSE and MAPE¶

# calculating the performance metrices like root mean squared error & mean absolute percentage error w.r.t. the actual data

Exponential smoothing methods¶

Since the dataset has only level & no trend & seasonality in the time series. So we will apply only the simple exponential smoothing technique for smoothing the time series data & the Holt Winter's additive or multiplicative methods would not be used.

Simple exponential smoothing¶

In [47]:
# importing the Simple Exponential Smoothing library 
from statsmodels.tsa.holtwinters import SimpleExpSmoothing

# creating a model using simple exponential smoothing algorithm on the training dataset of component failure
model = SimpleExpSmoothing(df_train['failure'])

# creating a new model fitting the trained model with 2% smoothing level for testing purpose
model_fit = model.fit(smoothing_level=0.2,optimized=False)

# checking the best parameters of the model
model_fit.params

# copying the test dataset into y_hat_ses dataframe
y_hat_ses = df_test.copy()

# forecasting the simple exponential smoothing model for the failure component from start to end date
y_hat_ses['ses_forecast'] = model_fit.predict(df_test.index.min(),
                                                        df_test.index.max())

Auto regression method (AR)¶

The AR model shows the autocorrelation between an observation with its previous observation (represented as lag p).PACF is the suitable chart that shows the correlation between the observations at different lags.

In [52]:
# importing ARIMA library from the statsmodels package

# applying the ARIMA algorithm on the component failure data of the train dataset with lag p=1
model = ARIMA(df_train['failure'], order=(1, 0, 0)) 

# fitting the ARIMA model & creating a new model for testing purpose
model_fit = model.fit()

# checking the best parameters of the fitted model

ARIMA¶

In [64]:
# import itertools library for iterating through the range to loop the values of p,d,q where d is the differencing lag
import itertools

# setting the range of p & q lags from 0 to 4
p=q=range(0,4)

# setting the range of d lags from 1 to 2
d=range(1,2)

# creating a list of the tuples of best values for each lags p,d,q
pdq=list(itertools.product(p,d,q))

# printing a title to fetch the list of p,d,q,values
print('Parameter combinations for the model')

# printing all the p,d,q values that needs to be iterated
for i in range(1,len(pdq)):
    print('Model {}'.format(pdq[i]))

The Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) lets you test how well your model fits the data set without over-fitting it.

The AIC score rewards models that achieve a high goodness-of-fit score and penalizes them if they become overly complex.

By itself, the AIC score is not of much use unless it is compared with the AIC score of a competing model.

The model with the lower AIC score is expected to strike a superior balance between its ability to fit the data set and its ability to avoid over-fitting the data set.

In [65]:
# creating a dataframe with column names param & AIC to print the parameters & Akaike Information Criterion

df_object1

# looping throigh the list of values of p,d,q lags & making ARIMA models to fit the training dataset for each lag
# printing the lag values along with their AICs
for param in pdq:
    try:
        mod = ARIMA(df_train['failure'], order=param)
        results_Arima = mod.fit()
        print(f'ARIMA:{param} - AIC:{results_Arima.aic}')
        df_object1 = df_object1.append({'param':param, 'AIC': results_Arima.aic},ignore_index=True)
    except:
        continue
